facts: Cloud computing = delivery of computing services over the internet (compute, storage, databases, networking, AI, IoT).
Public cloud avoids upfront hardware purchase: minimizes CapEx and ongoing datacenter operational costs.
Elasticity: scale resources up or down quickly as demand changes.
Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure stages: Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt (Migrate/Innovate), Govern, Manage.
First CAF stage is Define strategy.

pick.when: Extra resources while minimizing CapEx and OpEx
First stage of Cloud Adoption Framework

traps: CAF first stage is Strategy, not Plan or Ready.
Public cloud does not remove your responsibility for data and identities.

facts: Customer ALWAYS responsible for: data/information, devices, accounts and identities.
Provider ALWAYS responsible for: physical datacenter, physical network, physical hosts.
Varies by model: OS, network controls, applications, identity and directory infrastructure.
Customer responsibility order, most to least: On-premises, IaaS, PaaS, SaaS.
In SaaS, customer still owns data, accounts/identities and device access; provider runs the rest.

pick.when: Physical security of datacenter
Data, accounts, identities in any model
Patch the OS on a VM (IaaS)
Patch the OS in PaaS/SaaS

traps: Responsibility shared in SaaS: data, accounts, devices, identity - not the OS or app.
Physical hosts are never the customer's, even in IaaS.

facts: Public cloud: owned and operated by a third party; hardware shared between multiple tenants; no CapEx.
Private cloud: used by a single organization; hosted in own datacenter or by a third party; you keep the hardware.
Hybrid cloud: combines public and private (on-premises) environments.
You do not have to start with private to build hybrid; public plus on-premises is hybrid.
Multicloud: using multiple public cloud providers.
Azure Arc manages resources across on-premises, multicloud and edge; Azure VMware Solution moves VMware workloads to Azure.

pick.when: Hardware owned by third party, shared by multiple tenants
Burst capacity while keeping sensitive data on-premises
Single organization, own datacenter
Manage on-premises and other-cloud servers from Azure
Move VMware VMs from datacenter to Azure

traps: Private cloud still means you maintain the datacenter; cannot close it.
Hybrid does not require migrating from private first.

facts: Public: no CapEx, pay-as-you-go, rapid scaling, minimal maintenance of hardware.
Private: full control, strict compliance or data-residency needs, legacy systems that cannot move.
Hybrid: temporary demand spikes (burst to public) and extra security layers for sensitive data.
Hybrid allows keeping sensitive data on-premises while using public cloud for other workloads.
Multicloud: avoid vendor lock-in or use best service from each provider.

pick.when: Handle temporary increase in demand
Regulatory need to keep full control of hardware
Avoid capital expenditure on servers
Use more than one public provider

traps: Private cloud has higher cost and fewer cloud benefits, not lower cost.

facts: Consumption-based (pay-as-you-go): pay only for the resources you use; no upfront cost.
CapEx = upfront spend on physical infrastructure; value depreciates over time.
OpEx = ongoing spend on services over time; cloud is OpEx.
Migrating on-premises VMs to Azure pay-as-you-go shifts spending from CapEx to OpEx.
Consumption model: no upfront cost, no termination fees, stop paying when you stop using, billed per usage (often per second/minute).

pick.when: Pay only for what you use, no upfront cost
Buying servers and building a datacenter
Staff salaries, monthly usage bills

traps: Building datacenter infrastructure is CapEx, not OpEx.
Moving to Azure pay-as-you-go does not convert OpEx to CapEx.

facts: Pay-as-you-go: no commitment, billed on usage, highest per-unit price, most flexible.
Reserved Instances: commit 1 or 3 years for VMs and other resources; discount up to ~72%.
Azure Hybrid Benefit: reuse existing Windows Server/SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance to cut cost.
Spot VMs: use unused capacity at deep discount; can be evicted; for interruptible workloads.
Azure Pricing Calculator estimates cost of a planned solution; TCO Calculator compares on-premises vs Azure.

pick.when: Steady 24/7 workload, commit for 1 or 3 years
Reuse on-premises Windows Server license
Interruptible batch workload at lowest cost
Estimate monthly cost of planned Azure services
Compare on-premises cost to Azure

traps: Pricing Calculator estimates Azure cost; TCO Calculator compares vs on-premises.
Spot VMs can be evicted - not for critical workloads.

facts: Serverless: provider manages servers; you focus on code; scales automatically; pay only when code runs.
Azure Functions: event-driven, run small pieces of code on triggers (HTTP, timer, queue).
Azure Logic Apps: low-code/no-code workflows with connectors; also serverless.
Azure Event Grid is a serverless event routing service.
Servers still exist, but you do not provision or manage them.

pick.when: Run code in response to an event without managing servers
Automate email notification workflow by rule, low-code
Serverless computing in Azure

traps: Functions = code-first; Logic Apps = designer/connector workflows.
Serverless does not mean no servers; they are abstracted.

facts: High availability = maximum uptime; guaranteed through SLAs expressed as a percentage.
Higher SLA (99.99% vs 99.9%) means less allowed downtime; 100% is impractical and costly.
Vertical scaling (scale up/down): add or remove CPU/RAM on an existing VM.
Horizontal scaling (scale out/in): add or remove instances; handles increased demand.
Availability Zones protect against datacenter failure; availability sets protect against rack/host failure within a datacenter.
Elasticity/autoscale adapts resources automatically to demand.

pick.when: Service stays up if a datacenter fails
Increase VM size (more CPU/RAM)
Add more VM instances for more load
Automatically adjust instance count to demand
Spread VMs across racks inside one datacenter

traps: Zones = separate datacenters; availability sets = same datacenter.
Each Azure service has its own SLA; composite SLA is lower than individual ones.

facts: Reliability: ability to recover from failures and keep functioning; Azure Well-Architected Framework pillar.
Region pairs and Availability Zones keep workloads running if one location fails.
Azure Site Recovery replicates VMs to another region for disaster recovery.
Predictability covers performance (autoscale, load balancing, HA) and cost.
Azure Pricing Calculator and Cost Management help forecast spend.

pick.when: Disaster recovery for Azure VMs in another region
Keep servers available if a datacenter is offline long-term
pick.use: Region pair / replicate to another region

pick.when: Forecast cloud cost

traps: Zones protect within a region; region pairs/Site Recovery protect against region loss.

facts: Cloud providers offer built-in security tooling and compliance certifications.
Governance: use Azure Policy to enforce standards and assess compliance of resources.
Microsoft Defender for Cloud: posture management and threat protection across workloads.
IaaS gives most control and most security responsibility; PaaS/SaaS shift more to the provider.
Cloud supports governance via templates, policies, auditing and role-based access.

pick.when: Enforce organizational standards on resources
Assess security posture and protect workloads

facts: Management OF the cloud: autoscaling, templates/ARM-Bicep deployments, monitoring and alerts, auto-patching.
Management IN the cloud: portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs, APIs, Cloud Shell.
Templates (ARM/Bicep) deploy consistent environments repeatedly - infrastructure as code.
Azure Monitor and alerts provide visibility; Azure Advisor gives recommendations.
Azure Resource Manager is the deployment and management layer for all Azure tools.

pick.when: Deploy many identical custom VMs repeatedly
Manage Azure from command line

traps: Managing cloud resources via portal/CLI is management IN the cloud.

facts: IaaS: provider manages hardware, network connectivity, physical security.
Customer manages OS, patching, configuration, middleware, apps, data.
Azure Virtual Machines are the classic IaaS example.
Most flexible model and most customer management.
Use for lift-and-shift migration, test/dev environments, and apps needing OS-level control or legacy software.

pick.when: Lift-and-shift of on-premises server
Need to install and control the operating system
Legacy app/database moving to cloud
Custom apps with prerequisite software installed

traps: Azure SQL Database is PaaS; a SQL Server installed on a VM is IaaS.

facts: PaaS: provider also manages OS, middleware, runtime, development tools.
Customer manages applications and data.
Examples: Azure App Service, Azure SQL Database, Azure Functions.
PaaS gives no access to the underlying OS; least admin effort for hosting web apps among VM-vs-PaaS choices.
Fits development frameworks and analytics/business intelligence.

pick.when: Host web app with minimal administrative effort
Managed relational database, no server patching
Development framework without managing OS

traps: PaaS does not provide OS access; that is IaaS.
Azure Functions is serverless but also classed as PaaS.

facts: SaaS: provider manages everything except customer data, identities/access, and device posture.
Microsoft 365 (Exchange Online, Teams, etc.) is SaaS.
SaaS requires the least management from the customer.
Customer only configures the application and manages their data and users.
Dynamics 365 and Outlook.com are also SaaS.

pick.when: Minimize customer management responsibility
Microsoft 365
Hosted email/CRM used as-is

traps: Still customer-owned in SaaS: data, accounts/identities, devices.

facts: IaaS: Azure Virtual Machines, lift-and-shift, test/dev, full OS control.
PaaS: Azure App Service, Azure SQL Database; develop and host apps without managing OS.
SaaS: Microsoft 365, ready-made software over the internet.
Control and responsibility decrease IaaS > PaaS > SaaS; flexibility decreases too.
Azure SQL Database = PaaS; SQL Server on a VM = IaaS.

pick.when: Azure Virtual Machines
Azure App Service
Azure SQL Database
Microsoft 365
Lift-and-shift migration
Build and deploy apps without managing servers

traps: Do not classify Azure SQL Database as IaaS.
Dev frameworks and analytics fit PaaS, not SaaS.

facts: A region is a geographic area with one or more datacenters linked by a low-latency network.
Region pairs are in the same geography (except Brazil South), used for geo-replication and sequenced updates.
Sovereign regions are isolated Azure instances for compliance: Azure Government (US) and Azure China (21Vianet).
Azure Government is for US federal, state, local government entities and their contractors.
Azure China is operated by 21Vianet; Microsoft does not directly run those datacenters.

pick.when: Cloud for US government agency or contractor
Azure in mainland China, legal data residency
Geo-replication to a paired region in same geography

traps: Azure Government is not open to European or Canadian government contractors.
A region is not the same as an availability zone.

facts: AZs are physically separate datacenters within one region, each with independent power, cooling, networking.
Zone-enabled regions have a minimum of three zones; not all regions support AZs.
AZs protect against datacenter failure, not a whole-region failure.
Two or more VMs in different AZs give a 99.99% VM SLA; an availability set gives 99.95%.
AZs work with many services (VMs, disks, storage ZRS, etc.), not just VMs.

pick.when: Stay available if a single datacenter fails
pick.use: Deploy VMs across two or more availability zones

pick.when: 99.99% VM availability
Survive entire region failure

traps: AZs do not protect against a region failure.
Availability zones are not Azure regions.

facts: Azure datacenters are physical facilities Microsoft owns and operates worldwide.
Datacenters are grouped into regions, and within regions into availability zones.
Microsoft is responsible for physical security, power, cooling and networking (shared responsibility).
Customers choose the region where resources are deployed; datacenters themselves are not selectable.
traps: The customer is not responsible for physical datacenter security in IaaS, PaaS or SaaS.

facts: A resource is any manageable item in Azure (VM, VNet, database).
Every resource exists in exactly one resource group.
A resource group is a logical container; resources in it can be in different regions.
Resources can interact with resources in other resource groups.
Deleting a resource group deletes all resources in it; groups cannot be nested.

pick.when: Place a new VM in Azure
Remove all related resources at once

traps: A resource cannot be in two resource groups.
Resource groups cannot be nested, and do not limit resource region.

facts: A subscription is a unit of management, billing and scale; costs are reported per subscription.
A subscription trusts exactly one Microsoft Entra tenant; a tenant can have many subscriptions.
Need separate payment options per department: create a subscription for each.
Raise subscription limits/quotas by creating a new support request.
Resources (e.g. VMs) can be moved between subscriptions; a subscription is the first thing to create.

pick.when: Different payment option for each department
Increase subscription limits (e.g. SQL managed instances)
First thing to create when starting in Azure

traps: A support plan upgrade does not raise quotas; a support request does.
One subscription cannot trust multiple tenants.

facts: Management groups sit above subscriptions and organize them into a hierarchy.
Policies and RBAC applied to a management group are inherited by all its subscriptions.
Hierarchy supports up to six levels of depth, excluding the root and the subscription level.
Each directory has a single top-level root management group.

pick.when: Govern compliance/access across multiple subscriptions
Apply one policy to many subscriptions

traps: Resource groups cannot span subscriptions, so they are not for cross-subscription governance.

facts: Order top to bottom: management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, resources.
Settings (policy, RBAC) inherit downward through the hierarchy.
Segment departments using multiple subscriptions or multiple resource groups.
Regions do not define management boundaries; Entra directories are not used to segment departments here.

pick.when: Segment Azure for departments with separate admins
pick.use: Multiple subscriptions or multiple resource groups

pick.when: Governance above subscriptions

traps: Do not place resource groups above subscriptions in the order.

facts: VMs (IaaS): full OS control; you patch and manage the OS.
Containers virtualize the OS (not hardware); lightweight, fast to start, scale out.
ACI: simplest way to run a container without managing servers; AKS orchestrates containers at scale.
Azure Functions: serverless, event-triggered code, pay for execution, automatic scaling.
Azure Machine Learning builds/trains custom models; Azure AI services give prebuilt API-based AI.

pick.when: Run a container quickly without managing VMs
Orchestrate/manage many containers
Event-driven code, no server management
Full OS control, lift and shift
Build, test, deploy predictive models
Millions of IoT devices uploading data

traps: Functions is serverless but not a container manager.
Azure Virtual Desktop does not manage containers.

facts: VM scale sets: create and manage a group of identical load-balanced VMs that autoscale on demand or schedule.
Availability sets spread VMs across fault domains (power/network) and update domains (planned reboots); no extra cost.
Azure Virtual Desktop: cloud-hosted Windows desktops and apps, supports multi-session Windows.
Azure DevTest Labs: quickly create and remove many customized VMs for dev/test.
Spot VMs use unused capacity at a discount but can be evicted.

pick.when: Group of identical VMs that autoscale
Reduce impact of hardware failure or maintenance in a region
Deploy/remove 50 customized dev VMs weekly
Virtualized desktops and apps in the cloud
Cheap interruptible workloads

traps: Scale sets are not the dev/test lab answer.
Availability sets protect in a datacenter, not against datacenter failure (use AZs).

facts: Every VM needs a virtual network for its network interface.
A VM also needs compute size (vCPU/RAM) and disks (OS disk plus optional data disks).
A public IP address is optional, not required.
VM size drives vCPU, RAM, disk and network throughput.

pick.when: Additional resource required by a VM

traps: Public IP, service endpoint and Azure Firewall are not required for a VM.

facts: Azure App Service hosts web apps, API apps, WebJobs and mobile app backends (PaaS, HTTP-based).
Free and Shared tiers run on shared compute; Basic and above use dedicated VMs.
Standard tier and above add autoscale, deployment slots and custom domains/SSL.
Azure CDN caches content near users, best for global delivery of large video files.
Hosting options span a spectrum: VMs (IaaS), containers, App Service (PaaS), Functions (serverless).

pick.when: Host web app/API without managing servers
Best video playback for worldwide users
Web apps needing custom domains and autoscale
Full control of the hosting OS

traps: Traffic Manager and Application Gateway are not for content caching.
ExpressRoute is not an app delivery feature.

facts: VNet features: isolation and segmentation, internet access, Azure and on-premises connectivity, routing, filtering.
Site-to-Site VPN links on-premises VPN device to Azure VPN gateway over the internet, encrypted.
Point-to-Site VPN: individual client computer (remote workers) connects to a VNet.
ExpressRoute: dedicated private connection not over the internet; operates at OSI Layer 3.
NSGs filter traffic by IP, service tag or ASG; VNet peering connects VNets; Azure DNS hosts domains but can't register them.

pick.when: Remote workers connect to a VNet
Connect on-premises network to Azure over the internet
Private connection not crossing the internet
Limit connections between web and DB servers
Filter inbound to many VNets centrally
Separate network segment for a server
Represent on-premises VPN device in Azure
Protect websites from attacks, with reports

traps: NSG default rules exist and allow some traffic.
Traffic Manager is DNS-based load balancing, not VM internet access.
Azure DNS cannot buy domain names.

facts: Public endpoint: reachable over the internet via a public IP.
Service endpoint extends VNet identity to a service (e.g. Storage) over the Azure backbone, not the internet.
Private endpoint gives a service a private IP inside your VNet via Azure Private Link.
Service endpoints keep traffic off the public internet but the service keeps a public endpoint.

pick.when: Keep VNet traffic to Storage off the internet
Access PaaS service via private IP in your VNet

traps: An NSG or VPN Gateway does not route storage traffic privately; a service endpoint does.

facts: Five services: Blobs, Files, Queues, Disks, Tables.
Blobs: unstructured object storage; Files: SMB/NFS shares; Queues: async messaging; Disks: VM block storage; Tables: NoSQL key-value.
Map a network drive from Windows computers: Azure Files (File service).
Queue messages can be up to 64 KB each.
Cosmos DB: globally distributed multi-model NoSQL (JSON documents, multi-region writes).

pick.when: Map a network drive from Windows 10
Store unmanaged VM data disks
Async messaging between app components
Unstructured data: images, video, backups
JSON documents with multi-region writes
Large analytics data in Power BI, infrequent access

traps: A VM data disk is not a mappable network drive.
Azure SQL Database is relational, not for file shares.

facts: Blob access tiers: Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive.
Hot: frequently accessed, highest storage cost, lowest access cost.
Minimum retention: Cool 30 days, Cold 90 days, Archive 180 days.
Archive: lowest storage cost, highest retrieval cost and latency (hours); data is offline.
Archive can only be set per blob, not as the account default tier.

pick.when: Frequently read and written data
Infrequently accessed, kept at least 30 days
Lowest storage cost for rarely used data
Long-term backups, offline OK

traps: Archive is cheapest to store but costliest to retrieve.
Archive cannot be the account-level default.

facts: Azure always keeps 3 copies in the primary region.
LRS: 3 copies in one datacenter (minimum option); ZRS: 3 copies across 3 availability zones.
GRS: LRS in primary plus LRS in secondary = 6 copies; GZRS: ZRS primary plus LRS secondary = 6 copies.
Secondary region is read-only only with RA-GRS or RA-GZRS (read access).
Order least to most redundant: LRS, ZRS, GRS, RA-GRS, GZRS, RA-GZRS.

pick.when: Cheapest, protects against disk/rack failure
Survive datacenter failure within a region
Replicate to a paired region
Read data from secondary region before failover
Maximum resilience

traps: GRS is 6 copies, LRS is 3; do not confuse with GZRS count (also 6).
Plain GRS secondary is not readable until failover.

facts: Standard general-purpose v2 is the default type for blobs, files, queues and tables.
Premium types: block blobs, file shares (SMB and NFS), page blobs.
Account name: 3-24 chars, lowercase letters and numbers, globally unique.
Endpoint: https://<account>.<service>.core.windows.net (blob, file, queue, table, dfs for Data Lake Gen2).
Create a new file share under the Azure Files service in the storage account.

pick.when: Default for most scenarios
High-performance file shares, SMB and NFS
Low latency, small objects, high transactions
VM disks/page blobs only

traps: Data Lake Gen2 uses the .dfs endpoint, not .blob.

facts: AzCopy: command-line tool to copy blobs/files between storage accounts or from other sources; sync is one-way.
Storage Explorer: GUI app for Windows, macOS, Linux; uses AzCopy under the hood.
Azure File Sync: syncs an on-premises Windows file server with an Azure file share, bi-directional.
File Sync supports cloud tiering: hot files stay local, cold files in the cloud.
File Sync needs the Azure File Sync agent installed on Windows Server.

pick.when: Command-line copy to blob storage
GUI to manage blobs and files
Sync on-premises Windows file server with cloud

traps: AzCopy sync is not two-way; File Sync is.
Storage Explorer is not an on-premises sync tool.

facts: Azure Migrate: central hub to discover, assess and migrate servers, databases, web apps to Azure.
Azure Data Box: physical device shipped by Microsoft for offline bulk transfer (up to 80 TB per device).
Use Data Box when network bandwidth is too limited for online transfer.
Data Box supports import and export; disks are securely wiped after upload (NIST 800-88r1).

pick.when: Assess and migrate on-premises servers and apps
Move tens of TB offline, slow network
Export large data out of Azure physically

traps: Data Box is offline; Azure Migrate is online tooling.

facts: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is cloud identity and access management; no domain controllers or VMs needed
Entra ID uses REST/HTTPS protocols: SAML, OAuth, OpenID Connect - not Kerberos/NTLM/LDAP
Microsoft Entra Domain Services gives managed domain services: domain join, group policy, LDAP, Kerberos/NTLM
Entra Connect syncs on-premises AD identities to Entra ID (hybrid identity)
Entra ID is the identity provider for Microsoft 365, Azure portal and SaaS apps; supports dynamic group membership

pick.when: Sync on-premises AD accounts to the cloud
Legacy app needs LDAP/Kerberos/domain join without running DCs
Cloud identity provider for SaaS and Azure
Collect and analyze Entra ID security events automatically

traps: Entra ID is not Active Directory in the cloud: no group policy, LDAP or Kerberos (that is Domain Services)
Entra Connect syncs identities; it does not provide domain join

facts: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides what you can access
SSO: sign in once with one credential to access multiple apps/resources
MFA needs two or more of: something you know, have, or are
Passwordless options: Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator app, FIDO2 security keys
Self-service password reset (SSPR) lets users reset passwords without admin help; Entra Password Protection blocks weak passwords

pick.when: Sign in once to access many apps
Biometric or PIN tied to the device, no password
Physical USB/NFC key for passwordless sign-in
Users reset own forgotten password
Require a second verification factor

traps: Password plus security question is not MFA - both are 'something you know'
SSO does not add a second factor

facts: External identities let people outside your org access your resources using their own identity
B2B collaboration: invite guest users (partners) who use their own credentials to access your apps
B2C: Azure AD B2C is a customer identity and access management service for customer-facing apps
Microsoft Entra External ID is the newer offering covering workforce collaboration and customer scenarios
Guests sign in with their own work, school or social identity; you control their access

pick.when: Partners/vendors access your resources with their own credentials
Customers sign up/sign in to your consumer app with social accounts
pick.use: Azure AD B2C / External ID for customers

traps: B2B is for partners/guests; B2C is for customers of your own apps

facts: Conditional Access evaluates signals (user, location, device, app, risk) and applies if-then policies
Typical decisions: allow access, block access, or require MFA / compliant device / password change
Policies are enforced after first-factor authentication completes
Requires Microsoft Entra ID P1 or higher; risk-based policies need P2 (Identity Protection)
Security defaults are the free baseline that enforces MFA for everyone when not using Conditional Access

pick.when: Require MFA only when sign-in is from outside the corporate network
Block sign-ins from specific countries
Allow access only from compliant devices

traps: Conditional Access is not the first line of defence: it applies after the first factor
It is not RBAC: it controls sign-in, not resource permissions

facts: RBAC grants access through role assignments: security principal + role definition + scope
Scope hierarchy: management group > subscription > resource group > resource; permissions inherit downward
Built-in roles: Owner (full + assign access), Contributor (full, no assigning access), Reader (view only)
User Access Administrator manages user access to resources only
RBAC is allow-based and additive; it is enforced by Azure Resource Manager

pick.when: Create/manage all resources but cannot grant access
Full access including delegating access
View resources only
Manage who has access to Azure resources only

traps: Contributor cannot assign roles - only Owner/User Access Administrator can
RBAC controls resource actions; Azure Policy controls resource properties

facts: Zero Trust assumes breach: never trust, always verify, regardless of network location
Guiding principles: verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, assume breach
Every request is authenticated and authorized using all available data points
Six pillars: identities, devices, applications, data, infrastructure, networks
Replaces the idea of a trusted corporate network perimeter

pick.when: Verify every access request explicitly, even from inside the network
Limit user access with just-in-time and just-enough access

traps: Zero Trust is not perimeter/firewall-only security
Defense in depth is layered; Zero Trust is verify-everything - distinct models

facts: Defense in depth uses multiple layers so a breach of one layer does not compromise others
Layers outside-in: physical security, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, data
Physical security is the outermost layer; data is the innermost, what attackers ultimately want
Identity & access layer: SSO, MFA, Conditional Access, audit events
Perimeter: DDoS protection and firewalls; Network: segmentation, NSGs, deny by default

pick.when: Protect against DDoS at the network edge
Limit connectivity between resources with NSGs
Enforce MFA and Conditional Access

traps: Layers are ordered physical -> data; do not put identity after data
DDoS protection belongs to perimeter, not network or compute

facts: Defender for Cloud is a cloud security posture management (CSPM) and workload protection (CWPP) tool
Secure Score measures your security posture; higher score means fewer risks, with recommendations to improve
Gives security recommendations and threat alerts for Azure, on-premises and other clouds (multicloud)
Free tier covers CSPM basics; enhanced Defender plans add workload threat protection
Not a SIEM: Microsoft Sentinel is the SIEM/SOAR service

pick.when: Assess and improve security posture with Secure Score
Threat protection for servers, storage, SQL workloads
Collect and analyze security events across the enterprise (SIEM/SOAR)

traps: Defender for Cloud is not Sentinel: posture/protection vs SIEM/SOAR
Secure Score is about posture, not cost or compliance reporting

facts: Cost factors: resource type, consumption, maintenance, geography/region, network traffic, subscription type
Inbound (ingress) data transfer is free; outbound (egress) data is charged; data between zones/regions may be charged
Reservations (1 or 3 years) save up to ~72% on VMs vs pay-as-you-go
Azure Hybrid Benefit uses existing Windows Server/SQL licenses with Software Assurance to cut costs
Spot VMs use spare capacity at big discounts but can be evicted; auto-scaling and right-sizing reduce spend

pick.when: Reduce VM cost with a 1- or 3-year commitment
Reuse on-premises Windows Server licenses in Azure
Cheap interruptible workloads
Match resource size to actual use

traps: Inbound data transfer is free; outbound is what costs money
Hybrid Benefit needs Software Assurance or qualifying subscriptions

facts: Pricing calculator estimates the cost of Azure services you plan to deploy, before deployment
You configure services, region, tier and quantity to get a cost estimate you can export or share
TCO calculator (compare on-premises to Azure) has been retired; Pricing calculator is the estimating tool
It does not track actual spending; Microsoft Cost Management does that
Available publicly at azure.microsoft.com; no sign-in required

pick.when: Estimate monthly cost of planned Azure resources
Compare on-premises costs vs Azure migration
pick.use: TCO calculator (legacy) / Azure Migrate business case

traps: Pricing calculator is forecasting before deploy, not analysing past spend
Do not pick Cost Management for pre-deployment estimates

facts: Microsoft Cost Management monitors, allocates and optimizes costs for Azure (and AWS) in one place
Cost analysis shows current and past spend by resource, resource group, tag, subscription
Budgets set spending thresholds and trigger alerts when forecast or actual cost reaches them
Budgets alert; they do not stop or block resource usage by default
Azure Advisor gives cost recommendations (e.g. shut down idle VMs, buy reservations)

pick.when: Analyze and break down current spend
pick.use: Cost analysis in Microsoft Cost Management

pick.when: Get notified when spend crosses a threshold
Recommendations to lower costs
Estimate cost of planned deployment

traps: A budget does not cap or stop spending - it only alerts
Cost Management shows actual costs; Pricing calculator estimates future costs

facts: Tags are name/value metadata pairs applied to resources, resource groups and subscriptions
Used to organize resources for billing, cost reporting, ownership, environment (e.g. Dept=Finance)
Tags are not inherited by default; use Azure Policy to enforce or inherit them
A resource can have up to 50 tags
Tags can filter resources and group costs in Cost Management

pick.when: Group costs by department or project in billing reports
Require a tag on every new resource
Identify resources by environment or owner

traps: Tags do not control access (that is RBAC) and are not inherited automatically
Tags do not prevent deletion (that is resource locks)

facts: Microsoft Purview is a family of data governance, risk and compliance solutions
Unified data governance: map data estate, classify data, track lineage, data catalog
Risk and compliance: information protection, data loss prevention, eDiscovery, audit, insider risk
Service Trust Portal provides Microsoft compliance docs, audit reports and certifications
Compliance Manager (Purview) gives a compliance score and improvement actions

pick.when: Govern and catalog data across on-premises, multicloud and SaaS
Get Microsoft audit reports and compliance documentation
Assess compliance posture with a score

traps: Purview governs data; Defender for Cloud secures workloads
Service Trust Portal is documentation, not a policy enforcement tool

facts: Azure Policy enforces organizational standards and assesses compliance of resources at scale

facts: Resource locks prevent accidental deletion or modification of resources
